parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens if the micrometer does not read zero when fully closed. Would every reading for the wire be shifted the same way?
Hint 2: Think about what happens if you repeat the reading several times at different points along the wire or with slightly different tightness. Would you get exactly the same value each time?
parts.proper_answer: systematic errors: all readings are larger or smaller than the true value by a constant amount, e.g. due to zero error. random errors: readings show scatter about the true value.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Systematic Errors Shift Everything One Way**
Imagine your micrometer reads $0.02\text{ mm}$ even with nothing between the jaws. That is a zero error. Every time you measure the wire diameter you will add that extra bit on. So a systematic error means all your readings are consistently too big or consistently too small by the same fixed amount. It cannot be removed by averaging.

Step 2: **Random Errors Scatter Around the Truth**
Now imagine you measure the diameter at different places along the wire, or you tighten the screw a little differently each time. You might get $0.48\text{ mm}$, $0.50\text{ mm}$, $0.49\text{ mm}$. The values jump above and below the true value. That scatter is a random error. Taking an average of many repeats helps to reduce its effect.

parts.label: (b)
key_concepts: accuracy and closeness to true value
hints: Hint 1: Think about the instrument itself - what is the smallest change a micrometer screw gauge can actually show you, and what does that tell you about repeatability?
Hint 2: Think separately about the true diameter of the wire - what word describes whether your measured average is actually correct, even if your readings are very repeatable?
parts.proper_answer: precision: determined by the smallest division of the instrument, $0.01\text{ mm}$ for the micrometer, relates to repeatability and resolution. accuracy: how close the measured value is to the true value of the diameter.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Precision Is About How Finely You Can Read**
A micrometer screw gauge typically reads to $0.01\text{ mm}$. That small least count means you can get very repeatable, closely grouped readings. That is high precision. Precision is about resolution and consistency, not about being right. You can be precise but still wrong if there is a zero error.

Step 2: **Accuracy Is About How Close To True**
Accuracy means your result is actually close to the real, true diameter of the wire. You can have very precise readings all clustered at $0.55\text{ mm}$, but if the true diameter is $0.50\text{ mm}$ because of an uncorrected zero error, your measurement is precise but not accurate. Good accuracy needs systematic errors to be eliminated.
